alinaMoments.description: A professional portfolio and booking website for a family and newborn photographer, built solo with Next.js and TypeScript. The site is available in four languages via next-intl (German, English, Romanian, Italian) with locale-prefixed routing throughout, and integrates Cal.com for shoot bookings. A review system backed by Neon Postgres and Drizzle ORM lets clients submit testimonials, while Resend handles both the contact form and email notifications for new reviews. Rate limiting and the monthly-offer spot counter run on Upstash Redis in production, with a file-based store as a local development fallback. Animations use Framer Motion with Lenis smooth scrolling, creating an editorial, gallery-like browsing experience across the portfolio, services, and pricing sections. Styled with Tailwind CSS and deployed on Vercel.

chargeHub.description: A dashboard for managing electric-vehicle charging infrastructure, built solo to a 24-day plan (40+ merged pull requests) — the same domain as a product for charge-point operators. Station master data comes from the real Open Charge Map registry through a Nitro BFF layer (API key server-side only, cached); everything a registry doesn't provide — live charging status, historical sessions, KPIs — is simulated server-side deterministically, behind a swappable transport interface. Feature-first module structure with a repository pattern, Pinia for client state only, hybrid rendering per route. Above the classic filter bar sits a natural-language station search via Claude Haiku with structured output, grounded in real OCM IDs. DE/EN with localized routing, Vuetify theme via SCSS variables, accessibility with axe-core as a blocking CI gate. Tested with Vitest, @nuxt/test-utils and Playwright across four browsers/viewports (~92% coverage gate), plus an eval suite for the free-text search. GitHub Actions pipeline with lint, type-check, test, build, E2E and a Lighthouse gate with per-page thresholds; main protected by branch protection, Vercel deploy on every merge. Every significant decision is captured in an architecture decision record. Live and feature-complete.

join.description: Built collaboratively in a 5-person team, Join is a real-time Kanban task management application developed with Angular and Firebase. The board delivers live task synchronization via Firebase Firestore, user authentication, drag-and-drop workflow management across status columns, and a full contact system with task assignment, priority levels, and due dates. A summary dashboard provides an at-a-glance view of task statistics and upcoming deadlines. Working across five developers required coordinating component ownership, aligning on shared service interfaces, and Git workflows that mirror professional Angular development environments. After the team phase I kept maintaining my fork on my own: upgraded Angular 17 → 22 one major version at a time with the official migrations, replaced AngularFire with the official Firebase SDK, secured the database with Firestore security rules covered by emulator tests, added route guards, CI with CodeQL and a weekly health check, and brought npm audit findings from 97 down to 0. Fully responsive and deployed live.

elPolloLoco.description: A 2D jump-'n'-run built from scratch on the HTML5 Canvas 2D API — no game engine, no rendering library, zero runtime dependencies. Play as Pepe, a villager fighting off a flock of wild chickens across a parallax-scrolled desert: stomp enemies or throw collected salsa bottles, gather coins for extra lives, and take down the 200 HP Endboss, which runs its own walk → alert → attack → lunge state machine. The engine is class-based OOP on a shared DrawableObject → MovableObject inheritance chain, with custom gravity and jump physics and layered, per-interaction collision detection with damage cooldowns. A single requestAnimationFrame loop owned by the World advances the simulation in fixed 35 ms steps drawn from a delta-time accumulator, so gameplay stays frame-rate independent and a backgrounded tab can't burst-catch-up. A shared image pool decodes each sprite once and pre-warms it so the first frame never stalls on a cold decode, and icons and the background are sized to their actual on-screen resolution and shipped as WebP; every interval and timeout is torn down deterministically on game over or restart, and a Play Again button rebuilds the world in place without a page reload. The background track and effect pool load lazily instead of eagerly on page load, then effects play from a round-robin pool for zero restart latency, with a mute state persisted to localStorage. The pure game logic — collision boxes, jump validity, damage cooldowns, collectible pickup — is covered by 31 unit tests in a dependency-free node:test suite that loads the classic scripts into a node:vm sandbox, an asset-integrity test that scans every local src/href/url() in the repo, and 4 end-to-end tests with puppeteer-core that drive the system's installed Chrome or Edge — no bundled Chromium — pressing Play and asserting the canvas actually paints with no console errors: 36 tests in total, run in GitHub Actions on every push and pull request alongside lint and the build. Lint-clean against an ESLint 10 flat config, with JSDoc on every class and function. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages behind a strict Content-Security-Policy with no unsafe-inline, plus X-Frame-Options, Permissions-Policy, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy and long-lived immutable asset caching. Fully responsive, with on-screen touch controls that appear automatically on touch devices and a rotate-to-landscape prompt in portrait.

pokedex.description: An offline-first Pokédex PWA built in two phases: first entirely in vanilla JavaScript — no frameworks, just native browser APIs — to understand the platform from the ground up. Then migrated to TypeScript strict mode and Vite, without changing a single function. The Service Worker uses Workbox with separate caches for API responses (7 days, 300 entries) and sprites (30 days, 600 entries). Keyboard accessibility follows WAI-ARIA guidelines: focus trap inside the modal, ESC to close, arrow key navigation, and focus restoration to the previously active element. The holographic shimmer effect replicates physical trading cards: mouse position tracked via mousemove, injected into CSS custom properties --x/--y, and rendered through mix-blend-mode: color-dodge. 242 Vitest unit tests, a Playwright E2E suite (functional, accessibility via axe WCAG 2.1 AA, visual regression, and mobile), and ESLint with typescript-eslint strict ensure the correctness of the migrated codebase.

birthdayReminder.description: Conceived, designed, and built entirely solo — from initial idea to production deployment. This full-stack cross-platform app is structured across every layer: Angular 22 with NgRx spanning five independent state slices, an offline-first approach where IndexedDB is the single source of truth, and real-time cloud sync with Firebase Firestore via a pending-changes queue. The app ships as both a PWA with SSR on Cloudflare Pages and a native Android app via Capacitor, with push notifications delivered through both service workers and the native API. Google Calendar integration with OAuth 2.0 supports one-way and two-way sync with recurring events, alongside a full data pipeline for JSON, CSV, and vCard import/export. Quality is validated through Vitest unit tests, Cypress E2E and visual regression tests, and axe-core accessibility audits — with zero critical violations and full NVDA screen reader support.

familyCalendar.description: A weekly planner for families with several children: school, sports and music in one color-coded week that fits on exactly one printed A4 page. It started as a single HTML page and grew step by step into an Angular app. Activities are positioned by their real start time and sized by their duration, overlapping ones are laid out side by side, activities can be dragged to another day and time in 15-minute steps, and every change can be undone with Ctrl+Z. Before a PDF is captured, the day columns are resized to the proportions of a landscape A4 sheet, so every week fills exactly one page; the PDF libraries load only on the first export. The interface exists in English and Italian through build-time @angular/localize, where a missing translation fails the build, and titles are hyphenated with the rules of the interface language. Mihaela upgraded the app from Angular 17 to 22 with one commit per major version, moved the tests from Karma to Vitest (55 unit tests), added 125 Playwright end-to-end tests that run in CI on Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, also on an emulated Android phone and iPhone, and added versioned localStorage data with migrations plus JSON backup and import. State lives in signals, every component is OnPush, and the app runs zoneless, without zone.js. The whole week can be edited from the keyboard, every control has a name for screen readers, block text turns black or white to stay readable on any color, and axe-core checks every dialog against WCAG 2.2 AA. The live demo shows a fictitious family.
familyCalendar.shortDescription: Printable family week planner in Angular 22

todoApi.description: A 2-person team project where Mihaela owned the entire backend architecture from scratch. Built with Python 3.11, FastAPI 0.141, and SQLAlchemy 2.1, the API follows a strict four-layer architecture (Router → Service → Repository → Database) with Pydantic 2 for input validation and custom exception handling. Runs on SQLite locally and PostgreSQL in production, with ISO 8601 UTC timestamps and automatic schema creation on startup. A comprehensive test suite of 25 tests — 13 unit tests covering business logic and 12 integration tests — all pass against an in-memory SQLite database in under 0.2 seconds. Deployed live on Render with interactive Swagger/OpenAPI docs, paired with a React + TypeScript + Vite frontend.
todoApi.shortDescription: RESTful Todo API with clean layered architecture

secureNotesLab.description: A personal notes app built twice in Python and Flask: once with five intentional vulnerabilities, once fixed — to work through the full attack-and-defend cycle from the developer's side. The vulnerable version ships SQL injection in the login, stored XSS in note content, an IDOR on note viewing, plaintext password storage and missing CSRF protection on every state-changing form (OWASP Top 10:2025 A01, A04 and A05). The fixed version closes each one at the root: parameterized queries, Jinja2 auto-escaping, an ownership check that returns 403, Werkzeug password hashing and per-session CSRF tokens. Every exploit is documented step by step with its impact, and every fix with a before/after code comparison that explains the mechanism. Nine pytest tests prove the fixes hold: injection payloads are rejected, script tags render as plain text, other users' notes return 403 and requests without a valid CSRF token are refused. Security is part of the pipeline as well: GitHub Actions runs the tests, a Bandit static analysis scan and a pip-audit dependency scan as required checks on every pull request, main is branch-protected, and Dependabot keeps dependencies current. Runs locally only, by design.
secureNotesLab.shortDescription: OWASP Top 10 Lab: Vulnerable vs. Fixed

bfsgScanner.description: An open-source CLI, published to npm with SLSA provenance, that scans an entire site for WCAG 2.1 AA violations and maps every finding to the EN 301 549 / BFSG clause it breaks, producing a citable compliance report in JSON, HTML, or PDF. It exits with a non-zero code once violations pass a configurable severity threshold, so a CI pipeline can block a merge on accessibility. Page discovery runs from sitemap.xml, then a breadth-first crawl that respects robots.txt; each page is analyzed in a real Chromium via Playwright and axe-core, with a concurrency pool, per-host rate limiting, an identifiable User-Agent, and an optional settle delay so client-rendered pages are scanned once hydrated. The report.json output is described by a versioned JSON Schema and guarded by anti-drift tests with ajv. Built in TypeScript on Node.js, with 167 Vitest tests, CI across Linux, Windows and macOS, and developed as a sequence of small, individually reviewed pull requests; the thirteen decisions that shaped the architecture each carry an Architecture Decision Record. The release workflow publishes to npm via OIDC trusted publishing, with no long-lived token.

dineos.description: A restaurant operating system built solo end to end, as a product rather than a tutorial. Guests scan the QR code on their table, browse the menu in Italian, English or German with allergen filters, order from their own phone and follow each order live; the kitchen sees new orders on a real-time board the moment they are placed, and managers run tables, staff, menu and analytics from a dashboard. The FastAPI backend (async SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, Alembic) is multi-tenant: every query is scoped to its restaurant, backed by cross-tenant regression tests after a security review found and closed a leak. Real-time updates travel over authenticated WebSocket channels fanned out through Redis Pub/Sub, with per-IP and global connection caps. Payments use Stripe PaymentIntents with bill splitting, idempotency keys and a Redis dead-letter queue that retries failed webhooks with back-off. The Angular 21 frontend uses NgRx and serves four staff roles and anonymous guests from a single SPA. Load tests with k6 led to a rewrite of the menu endpoint that cut the median response under load from 0.7–1.4 s to 6–83 ms at 0.1 CPU and removed a 3 % error rate. Over 750 automated tests (pytest against real Postgres and Redis, Vitest, Playwright), 93 % backend coverage with a 90 % CI gate, mypy --strict, seven Architecture Decision Records, OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana and Sentry, and a CD pipeline that deploys every merge to a staging environment on Render and Neon.

normeon.description: A retrieval-augmented assistant for German technical documentation — regulations and Lastenhefte — that answers only with citations the backend has checked, and replies NICHT_GEFUNDEN instead of guessing. Built solo end to end. The FastAPI backend ingests PDF and DOCX files (with an OCR fallback for scanned pages) into PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector, chunks each document along its own sections, and retrieves with a hybrid of vector search, German full-text search and trigram matching, fused by Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Every source reaches the model as delimited, untrusted text; a citation the model invents is dropped, an answer left without a real one is withheld, and contradicting versions of the same requirement are flagged. Tenants are isolated twice — in the application's queries and by Postgres row-level security under a non-superuser role — behind JWT sign-in, with a dedicated security test suite. The Angular 22 frontend streams answers over SSE, turns every [S1] marker into a link to the cited passage, and uses API types generated from the OpenAPI document. Quality is measured, not claimed: a hand-written set of 50 German questions in five categories, an LLM judge checked against human scoring, and one setting changed per configuration with bootstrap confidence intervals. The deployed configuration finds a correct source in the top five for 39 of 40 answerable questions, declines all 10 unanswerable ones and cited no invented source in the evaluation. Over 700 tests in CI (Testcontainers against a real Postgres), mypy strict, five Architecture Decision Records, and a public demo on free tiers (Render, Neon, Gemini) with an encrypted nightly backup.
normeon.shortDescription: Cited RAG Assistant for German Technical Documents

caseStudyAlinaMoments.title: Alina Moments Photography
caseStudyAlinaMoments.subtitle: A full-stack website for a freelance photographer
caseStudyAlinaMoments.soloNote: Solo project: concept, development, production, and maintenance — from the first commit to the live deploy

intro.heading: Starting point
intro.body: Alina is a freelance photographer in Wolfsburg specializing in newborn, family, couple, and event photography. Before this project she had no website of her own — only an Instagram profile. The goal was a multilingual (DE/EN/RO/IT) professional website with online booking, a contact form, and a moderated review system — no CMS, no agency, no second developer on the team.
intro.body2: Every part of the stack — from the review database to the Content Security Policy to the CI pipeline and deployment — was designed, written, and shipped to production by a single person, held to the same bar a team would set for itself: a dedicated branch and pull request for every change, automated quality gates, end-to-end tests on every merge.

results.heading: Results — measured live today
results.performanceDetail: Desktop, measured against the production URL, same methodology as the CI gate: 40ms RTT, 10 Mbps, no CPU throttling
results.e2eTestsLabel: end-to-end tests in the CI pipeline (Playwright, 4 browser engines)
results.bundleSizeLabel: shared JS bundle (automated gate in CI)
results.methodologyNote: A methodology note that also appears in the original write-up: on a real mobile network with standard throttling, the performance score swings between roughly 53–73/100 — that reflects the actual cost of high-resolution images on a photography website, not a measurement error. The CI pipeline (production URL, desktop preset, median of 5 runs) consistently lands at 93–96/100.

liveFeatures.heading: What's live in production
liveFeatures.body: Online booking through Cal.com (lazy-loaded only on first hover/focus, so third-party cookies aren't loaded unasked), a contact form with Zod validation and email delivery via Resend, page-specific OG images, sitemap/robots, a PWA manifest, native dark mode, and four languages with correct hreflang.

testimonial.heading: A real, published review
testimonial.quote: “A shoot at its finest: no stiff poses, just real laughter and real faces. The photos look like they're straight out of a reel, only better. Everything happened in a flash and the result is amazing. These aren't photos, they're real memories. Rating: 10/10”
testimonial.author: Giuseppe, birthday shoot
testimonial.flow: The full flow is real: the client submits a review through the public form → the system writes a row with status pending to Postgres (Neon) → a moderation email with an HMAC-signed link goes out (one-click approve/reject, no sensitive data in the token) → once approved, the review is published and the homepage is revalidated via revalidateTag. Tested live on June 1, 2026 with a real review, confirmed by the client. Current state of the database (as of September 2026): 5 approved, 1 pending review — a modest but real number, growing organically since go-live, and the infrastructure has stayed verified and production-ready throughout.

engineering.heading: Engineering, not just design
engineering.item1Title: A “harmless” Node import broke the CSP on every page.
engineering.item1Body: lib/utils.ts imported Node's crypto.timingSafeEqual in the same file that exports cn() — the CSS class utility used by every client component. As a result, Next.js also bundled the vm-browserify polyfill (which uses eval() internally) into every browser bundle, violating the strict-dynamic CSP. Found through empirical bisection (progressively stubbing components and inspecting the compiled chunks), not by guessing. Fix: moved the function into a server-only module. Lighthouse Best Practices: 78 → 100 (CI).
engineering.item2Title: Rate limiting could be bypassed under concurrency.
engineering.item2Body: The rate limiter ran get and set as two separate steps (TOCTOU) — concurrent requests could slip past the limit before the counter updated. Fix: atomic kv.incr(), for both Vercel KV and the local dev fallback.
engineering.item3Body: Moderation tokens and admin secrets were compared with === across four different endpoints — theoretically vulnerable to timing attacks. Fix: a central timingSafeStringEqual(), used everywhere a secret is checked.
engineering.item4Title: Two parallel E2E runs were blocking each other.
engineering.item4Body: The concurrency gate in ci.yml compared github.ref (push event) against github.head_ref (pull request event) — two values that never match. Result: every commit triggered two simultaneous E2E runs on the same shared runners, with intermittent timeouts on WebKit (reproduced live: same commit, one run green in 9:42, the other red in 16:51, running at the same time). Fix: github.ref_name instead of github.ref. Verified: the duplicate run is now cancelled within 2 seconds.
engineering.item5Title: API routes were silently redirected under the locale prefix.
engineering.item5Body: The i18n middleware didn't exclude /api/* from its matcher: with localePrefix: "always", every call to /api/admin/reviews was silently redirected to /de/api/admin/reviews (which doesn't exist). Discovered by manually checking that an expected 401 status actually came from the app code and not from Vercel. Fix: explicitly excluded api from the next-intl matcher.

honestStatus.heading: Honest status, not a mockup
honestStatus.item1: Live since June 1, 2026 — no staging environment: public domain, real database, real transactional emails.
honestStatus.item2: No custom domain — a deliberate, confirmed decision by the client, not a technical limitation.
honestStatus.item3: Single-author repository — all pull requests were opened by the same person, checked by the CI gate, and merged; no second person did code review.
honestStatus.item4: Review volume is still modest — 5 approved, 1 in moderation: growing organically since go-live, but the flow is not yet tested at real scale.

caseStudyBfsgScanner.title: bfsg-scanner
caseStudyBfsgScanner.subtitle: An accessibility scanner for WCAG 2.1 AA / EN 301 549 / BFSG
caseStudyBfsgScanner.soloNote: Open-source side project: concept, architecture, implementation, tests, CI/CD, release, and documentation — single developer.
caseStudyBfsgScanner.period: 2026 — v0.1.0 published to npm on September 1, 2026; v0.2.0 on September 10, 2026; v0.2.2 on September 29, 2026; v0.3.0 on October 17, 2026; v0.4.0 on October 19, 2026; v0.4.1 on October 24, 2026; v0.4.2 on November 13, 2026; v0.4.3 on November 24, 2026

intro.heading: Context / problem
intro.body: Since June 28, 2025 the BFSG (Barrierefreiheitsstärkungsgesetz) has made digital accessibility a legal requirement in Germany for many B2C businesses: e-commerce, banking, bookings, ticketing. Anyone who builds or operates these sites has to be able to demonstrate conformance.
intro.body2: The existing tools (axe, Lighthouse) return rule IDs, not legal citations, and analyze one page at a time. bfsg-scanner scans a whole site and maps every finding to the EN 301 549 / BFSG clause it breaks, producing a citable compliance report in JSON, HTML, or PDF.

whatItDoes.heading: What it does
whatItDoes.item1: Discovers the site's pages — sitemap.xml first, then a breadth-first crawl that respects robots.txt, with a configurable page limit. Sitemap entries on another host are flagged instead of silently dropped, and a staging build can be scanned against the production sitemap.
whatItDoes.item2: Analyzes every page in a real Chromium via Playwright + axe-core, with a concurrency pool, per-host rate limiting, an identifiable User-Agent, and an optional settle delay so client-rendered pages are scanned once hydrated.
whatItDoes.item3: Maps each violation to its WCAG 2.1 success criterion and the corresponding EN 301 549 clause — and, via § 4 BFSG, to the statutory presumption of conformity. Since v0.4.0 the default rule set also covers the Level A criteria WCAG 2.1 added, such as SC 2.5.3 Label in Name; on this portfolio it caught 13 elements whose accessible name did not contain their visible label.
whatItDoes.item4: Produces the report as report.json (versioned JSON Schema), report.html (DE/EN, self-contained file), and report.pdf (A4, to be archived as a record).
whatItDoes.item5: Exits with a non-zero code once violations reach a configurable severity threshold, so a CI pipeline can block a merge on accessibility.

results.heading: In numbers
results.pullRequestsLabel: merged pull requests, each reviewed on its own
results.osLabel: operating systems in CI — Linux, Windows, macOS
results.exitCodesLabel: documented semantic exit codes, with a reasoned hierarchy so CI knows why it stopped
results.reportFormatsLabel: report formats, from the same run
results.provenanceLabel: provenance on npm via OIDC trusted publishing — no long-lived token in the release workflow
results.demoViolationsLabel: violations found on the W3C's deliberately inaccessible demo site
results.demoViolationsDetail: across 5 pages — 11 critical, 13 serious — each with its WCAG criterion and EN 301 549 clause, in a single PDF
results.mappingLabel: every finding mapped from its WCAG 2.1 criterion to the EN 301 549 / BFSG clause

highlights.heading: Technical highlights
highlights.item1Title: Published to npm with SLSA provenance.
highlights.item1Body: The release workflow publishes via OIDC trusted publishing — no long-lived token anywhere in it — with npm 2FA on the account.
highlights.item2Title: Small pull requests, each reviewed on its own.
highlights.item2Body: Each one does a single thing; the thirteen decisions that shaped the architecture also have an Architecture Decision Record.
highlights.item3Title: 167 tests, CI on three operating systems.
highlights.item3Body: The Vitest suite runs on Linux, Windows, and macOS on every push.
highlights.item4Title: The output is a stable contract, not an ad-hoc format.
highlights.item4Body: A versioned JSON Schema describes report.json, guarded by anti-drift tests with ajv so the shape can't silently change.
highlights.item5Body: Documented with a reasoned hierarchy, so a pipeline can tell an accessibility failure apart from a crawl error, a usage mistake, or a broken runner.
highlights.item6Body: docs/SCANNING-ETHICS.md — scan only sites you own or are authorized to test; rate limiting, robots.txt, and an identifiable User-Agent are on by default.

demoResult.heading: Demonstrated result
demoResult.body: Run against the W3C's deliberately inaccessible demo site → 24 violations across 5 pages (11 critical, 13 serious), each with its WCAG criterion and EN 301 549 clause, in a single PDF.

learned.heading: What I learned
learned.item1: Real release engineering: provenance, OIDC trusted publishing, npm 2FA, publish-on-tag.
learned.item2: Designing the output as a stable contract (versioned JSON Schema), not an ad-hoc format.
learned.item3: Controlled concurrency and scanning "netiquette" — rate limiting, robots.txt, an identifiable UA.
learned.item4: Translating legal requirements (BFSG → EN 301 549 → WCAG) into verifiable, tested logic.

caseStudyDineos.subtitle: A restaurant operating system: QR ordering, a live kitchen display and Stripe payments
caseStudyDineos.soloNote: Personal project, built alone: product concept, architecture, backend, frontend, infrastructure, deployment and documentation.
caseStudyDineos.period: June to November 2026. Version 1.0 released on October 19, 2026, version 1.0.1 on November 9, 2026
caseStudyDineos.demoNote: guest view of a demo table, no sign-up needed. The free server can take up to two minutes to wake up.

intro.heading: Context / problem
intro.body: In many restaurants an order still travels on paper: the waiter writes it down, carries it to the kitchen, and the guest waits for the bill. Every step depends on someone being free, and the kitchen only learns about an order when the slip arrives.
intro.body2: DineOS moves that flow onto the guest's own phone. A QR code on the table opens the menu without an account or an app; the order reaches the kitchen display the moment it is placed, the guest watches it move from received to ready, and pays at the table. One deployment serves many restaurants, and each one sees only its own data.

whatItDoes.heading: What it does
whatItDoes.item1: The guest scans the table's QR code and gets an anonymous session for that table: no account, no app to install. The menu comes in Italian, English or German, with allergen filters.
whatItDoes.item2: An order reaches the kitchen in real time. The kitchen display is a board with four columns (new, confirmed, preparing, ready) fed over WebSocket, and every status change appears on the guest's phone straight away.
whatItDoes.item3: Guests can call a waiter and ask for the bill from their phone. The bill can be paid by card through Stripe or split between several people.
whatItDoes.item4: Managers see every table at a glance (free or occupied, open orders, running total), print QR codes, manage staff with four roles (kitchen, waiter, manager, admin) and follow revenue, top dishes and peak hours.
whatItDoes.item5: Admins maintain the menu with translations per language and allergen tags. Changes reach guests through a cache that is invalidated per restaurant.

results.testsDetail: pytest against real PostgreSQL and Redis, Vitest, Playwright end to end
results.medianDetail: 50 concurrent users at 0.1 CPU, down from 0.7–1.4 s

highlights.heading: Technical highlights
highlights.item1Title: Tenant isolation, learned the hard way.
highlights.item1Body: Multi-tenancy came after the core features were built, and a security review I ran found the gap this left: two billing endpoints did not check the restaurant, so a manager who knew another restaurant's session ID could read or create its bills. Every repository query is now scoped to the restaurant, and cross-tenant tests check that another restaurant's data answers with 404.
highlights.item2Body: WebSocket messages go through Redis Pub/Sub, so a guest connected to one worker still hears about an order handled by another. Every channel checks its token: the table channel accepts only the token of its own session, the kitchen channel only active staff. Connections are capped per IP and globally, and a heartbeat closes dead sockets.
highlights.item3Title: Payments that do not get lost.
highlights.item3Body: Stripe PaymentIntents with idempotency keys, so a retried request never charges twice. When processing a webhook fails, the event goes to a dead-letter queue in Redis and a scheduled worker retries it with exponential back-off; an admin API shows what is left and retries or discards it. Every billing action is written to an audit log.
highlights.item4Title: Load tests that changed the code.
highlights.item4Body: A k6 script runs the real guest flow with 50 concurrent users. It showed that the cached menu was still turned into objects, validated and serialized again on every request. Serving the cached bytes as they are, and letting requests wait for a free Redis connection instead of failing, brought the median from 0.7–1.4 s down to 6–83 ms at 0.1 CPU, with no failed requests.
highlights.item5Title: Bugs that only show up in a real setup.
highlights.item5Body: The daily report was emailed twice, because each of the two uvicorn workers started its own scheduler; a claim in Redis with SET NX now lets exactly one of them send it. The kitchen sometimes missed new orders, because the event was published before the order was committed; the commit now comes first, and a test checks the order of the two.
highlights.item6Body: OpenTelemetry traces, Prometheus metrics with Grafana dashboards, structured logs and Sentry, from local development to staging. Every merge to main deploys to staging and runs a smoke test, and a deploy hook that answers without a real deploy ID now fails the pipeline. Production is a manual promotion of a tested staging build: prepared, and deliberately kept for the first paying restaurant.

finding.heading: The most useful lesson
finding.body: A green test suite and a green pipeline did not mean the system worked. The most serious bugs only appeared on a real server: a Stripe webhook that answered 200 but never committed its write, two refresh tokens issued in the same second that came out identical, and a deploy hook that answered "Accepted" for three months while the staging site kept serving a build from July. Since then I check every change on staging by running the real flow, not only by reading CI.

learned.heading: What I learned
learned.item1: The tenant boundary belongs in the first migration. Adding it later meant touching almost every repository, and that is how the gap slipped in.
learned.item2: Measure first, then set targets. The first targets for coverage and image size came from a plan written before any code existed; the ones that held came from measurements.
learned.item3: Every free-tier limit is a date in the calendar. Render's free database expired after 30 days and took staging down; staging now runs on Neon, with a weekly keep-alive check.
learned.item4: Write decisions down while they are fresh. Seven ADRs explain why WebSocket instead of polling, why anonymous table sessions instead of guest accounts and why one Angular app for every role.

caseStudyNormeon.title: Normeon
caseStudyNormeon.subtitle: A RAG assistant for German technical documentation that cites its sources
caseStudyNormeon.soloNote: Personal project, built alone: concept, architecture, backend, frontend, evaluation, deployment and documentation.
caseStudyNormeon.period: August to November 2026. Version 1.0 released on November 9, 2026, version 1.2 on November 16, 2026
caseStudyNormeon.periodNote: live demo with guest access, no sign-up needed

intro.heading: Context / problem
intro.body: Engineers in the automotive industry work with long German documents: regulations such as the StVZO, and Lastenhefte that change from one version to the next. A general chatbot answers fluently, but it cannot show where a value comes from, and it guesses when the documents say nothing.
intro.body2: Normeon answers only from the documents a team has uploaded. Every statement carries a citation that the backend has checked against the retrieved passages. When the documents do not contain the answer, it says so instead of guessing. The demo corpus holds two public regulations (StVZO and FZV) and two versions of a synthetic Lastenheft that contradict each other on purpose.

whatItDoes.heading: What it does
whatItDoes.item1: Reads PDF and DOCX files, with OCR for scanned pages, and splits each document along its own sections. Version and validity dates are stored with every document.
whatItDoes.item2: Searches in three ways at once: by meaning (vector search with pgvector), by words (German full-text search) and by codes such as LH-3.2.1 (trigram matching). The three rankings are merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
whatItDoes.item3: Passes the best passages to the language model as numbered sources. They are marked as untrusted data, so text inside a document cannot give the model instructions.
whatItDoes.item4: Checks every citation in the answer. A source number the model made up is removed, and an answer left without a real citation becomes NICHT_GEFUNDEN. When two versions of a requirement disagree, the answer names both.
whatItDoes.item5: Streams the answer to an Angular app. Each citation opens the cited passage; where the original file is stored, the PDF page opens with the passage highlighted.

results.recallDetail: deployed configuration, measured on the evaluation set

highlights.heading: Technical highlights
highlights.item1Body: Fifty German questions written by hand, ten per category, including questions the documents cannot answer and questions about contradicting versions. Each configuration changes one setting, and every result comes with a bootstrap confidence interval. I checked the automatic judge against my own scores: it agreed on 15 of 15 questions.
highlights.item2Title: Chunks follow the document, not a fixed size.
highlights.item2Body: Splitting by section instead of fixed 500-token windows raised recall by 35 points. The decision and the numbers are written down in an ADR.
highlights.item3Body: Vector search alone cost 8 points of answer accuracy. Full-text search alone found a correct source for only 6 of 40 questions. Together, with rank fusion, they find one for 39 of 40.
highlights.item4Body: Each company only sees its own documents. This is enforced in the application's queries and again by PostgreSQL row-level security under a role without superuser rights. A separate security test suite checks each layer on its own.
highlights.item5Body: A document cannot close its source block, forge another source's citation or rewrite the prompt. The tests even use a deliberately obedient fake model: when it follows an instruction hidden in a document, no document name leaks into the answer. Uploads are checked before they are stored: oversized files, encrypted PDFs and zip bombs are refused.
highlights.item6Title: A public demo at zero cost.
highlights.item6Body: Render, Neon and the Gemini free tier, with a rate limit per IP address and a daily question cap. A nightly database backup is encrypted before it is stored, and restoring it was tested on a separate database.

finding.heading: The most useful result
finding.body: Retrieval is not the bottleneck. Nine of the demo's ten wrong answers are refusals, and in eight of them the right source was already in the context. Before reaching for a bigger model, I measured the cheaper fixes: a prompt that allows partial answers brought no measurable gain, and adding neighbouring passages could help at most 2 of 50 questions. The remaining lever is a larger model, which does not fit the free tier, so it is documented as a known limit.

learned.heading: What I learned
learned.item1: An evaluation set is worth more than any single feature. Some of my assumptions were wrong: the reranker lowered recall with the hosted embeddings, and ten passages of context gave worse answers than five.
learned.item2: Security in a RAG system is mostly about data: who may see which document, and what a document is allowed to do to the model.
learned.item3: Constraints shape the architecture. The free tier meant no PyTorch in the image and hosted embeddings, and each change was measured again before it went live.
learned.item4: A negative result is a result. The over-refusal issue was closed with a measured upper bound, not with a guess.

caseStudyBirthdayReminder.title: Birthday Reminder Pro
caseStudyBirthdayReminder.subtitle: An offline-first birthday manager for web and Android, with optional cloud sync and Google Calendar integration
caseStudyBirthdayReminder.soloNote: Personal project, built alone: concept, architecture, frontend, cloud integration, testing, CI/CD, deployment and documentation.
caseStudyBirthdayReminder.period: August 2025 to November 2026. Version 1.0 released on July 12, 2026, version 1.4.3 on November 16, 2026
caseStudyBirthdayReminder.periodNote: live demo without an account, demo data with one click

intro.heading: Context / problem
intro.body: Birthdays end up scattered across phone contacts, social networks and calendars. A reminder app is only useful if it keeps working when the network does not, and if nobody has to create an account just to try it.
intro.body2: Birthday Reminder Pro stores every entry on the device first, in IndexedDB, and works fully offline. Signing in with Google is optional: it adds sync across devices through Firestore and two-way sync with Google Calendar. The same Angular code runs as a prerendered PWA on Cloudflare Pages and as an Android app built with Capacitor.

whatItDoes.heading: What it does
whatItDoes.item1: Manages birthdays with photos, notes, categories, search, age and zodiac sign. Everything is written to IndexedDB first, so the app works without a connection and without an account.
whatItDoes.item2: Syncs across devices after an optional Google sign-in. Changes made offline wait in a pending-changes queue and are sent to Firestore when the connection returns.
whatItDoes.item3: Syncs with Google Calendar one way or both ways, as yearly recurring events, including later edits and deletions.
whatItDoes.item4: Sends reminders as browser notifications through the service worker and as native notifications on Android, with scheduled messages that fill in the person's name and age.
whatItDoes.item5: Imports JSON, CSV and vCard, exports JSON and CSV, and shows statistics, category counts and the monthly distribution of birthdays. The interface is available in English and Italian, with a dark mode.

results.heading: In numbers
results.unitTestsDetail: Vitest in browser mode, real Chromium
results.e2eTestsLabel: Cypress end-to-end tests, including accessibility checks with axe-core
results.rulesTestsLabel: tests for the Firestore and Storage security rules, run against the emulator
results.coverageDetail: CI fails below 91 % statements or 89 % branches
results.bundleLabel: main bundle; CI fails above 500 KB
results.pullRequestsLabel: merged pull requests, each checked by CI

highlights.heading: Technical highlights
highlights.item1Title: Offline-first, with the device as the source of truth.
highlights.item1Body: Every write goes to IndexedDB first and updates the NgRx store optimistically, with a backup to roll back on failure. Firestore is a replica, not the primary store. The trade-off is written down: conflicts are resolved by the most recent update, not merged field by field.
highlights.item2Title: Firebase only for people who sign in.
highlights.item2Body: The Firebase SDK is never imported statically. A small cookie set at sign-in (Secure, SameSite=Strict, no secret in it) tells the app at startup whether to load it, so visitors without an account never download it. A Cypress test checks this.
highlights.item3Body: 50 tests for the Firestore rules and 22 for the Storage rules run against the Firebase emulator in CI. App Check with reCAPTCHA Enterprise protects the backend. A CI script checks the Content Security Policy and fails when an image host is allowed in img-src but missing from connect-src: that gap once made the service worker answer 504 for blocked photos.
highlights.item4Body: Every pull request runs lint, type checks, unit tests with coverage gates, Cypress end-to-end tests, a visual regression report on 18 screens, Lighthouse CI (accessibility and SEO at least 0.9) and a bundle budget. npm run ci:local runs the same chain locally.
highlights.item5Body: semantic-release derives the version and the changelog from conventional commits, and every release on main is deployed to Cloudflare Pages. Dependabot patch and minor updates are merged once CI is green. A weekly health check reviews workflows, vulnerabilities and the live site, and opens a single issue when something needs attention.
highlights.item6Body: The birthday list jumped while scrolling. Tracking each row's offset on the live site counted 60 jumps of up to 196 px at a width of 768 px. Rows had different heights, while the virtual scroll assumed a fixed one. After the fix, the same measurement showed 0 jumps at all three tested widths, and every row had the expected height at 20 widths from 320 to 1920 px.

finding.heading: The most useful result
finding.body: A real account had 1004 documents in Firestore for 61 people. Deduplication only cleaned the list shown on screen: local copies with a new ID were uploaded again, the losing cloud copies were never deleted, and the real-time listener brought them back. On top of that, every sign-in ran the merge twice. The fix deletes the losing copies only after the survivors are saved, never deletes while offline, and runs one merge per user. Affected accounts clean themselves up on their next sign-in, and each of these cases is covered by tests.

learned.heading: What I learned
learned.item1: Offline-first moves the hard part into synchronisation. The most serious bug in the project was not in the interface but in merging local and cloud data.
learned.item2: A number makes a bug discussable. Measuring the scroll jumps and counting the duplicate documents turned vague reports into fixes that can be verified.
learned.item3: Free tiers shape the scope, and limits belong in the documentation. Cloud photo storage needs a paid Firebase plan, so it sits behind a feature flag and photos stay on the device in the demo. Google Calendar access is capped at 100 users until Google verifies the app. Both are documented as known limitations.
learned.item4: A long-running project needs maintenance as a process. The app started on Angular 17 and now runs on Angular 22 with zoneless change detection, kept current by Dependabot, automated releases and a weekly health check.

caseStudyChargeHub.title: ChargeHub
caseStudyChargeHub.subtitle: An operations dashboard for an EV charge-point operator
caseStudyChargeHub.soloNote: Solo project: architecture, implementation, tests, CI/CD, and deployment — a single developer, held to a team's bar.

intro.heading: Starting point
intro.body: A charge-point operator needs an operational view of its network: where the stations are, which ones are online, how much energy and revenue they produce. ChargeHub is that dashboard, built solo as a portfolio project in the same problem domain. Station master data comes from a real public registry, Open Charge Map; everything a public registry can't provide — live status, charging sessions, KPIs — is generated by a deterministic server-side simulation.
intro.body2: It is built to the bar a team would set for itself: a branch and pull request for every change, branch protection on main, and a CI pipeline that lints, type-checks, tests behind a coverage gate, builds, runs Playwright across four browsers and viewports, and holds every page to its own Lighthouse budget. Every significant decision has an Architecture Decision Record.

whatItDoes.heading: What the dashboard does
whatItDoes.item1: Lists and maps real charge points from the Open Charge Map registry, fetched through a server-side BFF route that keeps the API key off the client and caches the responses.
whatItDoes.item2: Shows live status, power draw, and current sessions per station — produced server-side by a deterministic simulation that sits behind a swappable transport interface, so a real telemetry feed can replace it without touching the UI.
whatItDoes.item3: Aggregates historical sessions into KPIs and time-series charts — utilisation, energy delivered, revenue — rendered with Chart.js.
whatItDoes.item4: Lets an operator search the fleet in plain language ("fast CCS chargers over 150 kW from Ionity that are online"): Claude Haiku 4.5 returns a structured filter, validated with Zod and grounded in real station IDs.
whatItDoes.item5: Separates an operator role (manage tariffs) from a read-only viewer role, with server-side sessions and localized DE / EN routing.

results.heading: In numbers
results.pullRequestsLabel: merged pull requests, each on its own branch behind branch protection
results.adrLabel: Architecture Decision Records (docs/adr) — design system, telemetry simulation, live-update transport, module structure, Pinia scope, rendering strategy, AI search
results.coverageLabel: unit-test coverage gate, enforced in CI (Vitest + @nuxt/test-utils)
results.evalLabel: hand-labelled queries in the eval suite for the natural-language search
results.perfLabel: Lighthouse Performance on the station detail page: initial score → blocking CI gate
results.perfDetail: throttled mobile, 3-run median in Lighthouse CI
results.a11ySeoLabel: Lighthouse Accessibility · SEO, required on every page (CLS < 0.1 everywhere)

aiSearch.heading: Natural-language station search
aiSearch.body: Above the normal filter bar, an operator can type a request instead of clicking through dropdowns. Claude Haiku 4.5 returns a structured object — not free text — which is validated against a Zod schema and applied to the same filter state the UI controls use. Station references are constrained to real Open Charge Map IDs, so the model can't invent a location. The feature is optional: with no API key the dashboard runs exactly as before, just with the classic filters.

highlights.heading: Engineering, not just a demo
highlights.item1Title: The API key never reaches the browser.
highlights.item1Body: Open Charge Map is called only from a Nitro server route that injects the key and caches the response; the client receives a narrowed, typed payload and never sees a credential.
highlights.item2Title: Simulated telemetry — but deterministic and stateless.
highlights.item2Body: ADR 0002: live status and history are derived from station ID plus timestamp, so every serverless invocation returns the same value with no shared state. ADR 0003: the whole feed sits behind one interface (polling, not WebSocket) that a real source can implement later.
highlights.item3Title: Station detail performance rebuilt from 46 to the CI gate.
highlights.item3Body: The station detail page started at 46/100 on throttled mobile. MapLibre is now lazy-loaded on demand, the icon set was cut from a 403 kB webfont to a 3.7 kB subset, and responses ship Brotli-compressed — enough to hold ≥ 82/100 as a blocking Lighthouse CI check.
highlights.item4Title: Per-page Lighthouse budgets, not one global number.
highlights.item4Body: Each route carries its own thresholds — station detail ≥ 82, dashboard ≥ 80, analytics ≥ 78, sessions ≥ 70, with Accessibility 100 and CLS < 0.1 everywhere — measured as a 3-run median in CI.
highlights.item5Title: The natural-language search has its own eval suite.
highlights.item5Body: 19 hand-labelled queries check that the model's structured output maps to the right filters. It runs on demand, deliberately outside CI, because each run has an API cost.
highlights.item6Title: Every architectural decision is written down.
highlights.item6Body: Seven ADRs cover the design system, telemetry simulation, live-update transport, module structure, Pinia scope, per-route rendering, and the AI search — each with the context and the trade-off, not just the outcome.

limitations.heading: Honest limitations
limitations.item1: Telemetry is simulated. It is deterministic and swappable, but there is no real hardware or live feed behind it.
limitations.item2: Authentication is mocked — two hard-coded accounts (operator, viewer). Enough to demonstrate role separation, not a real identity system.
limitations.item3: Station detail pages don't use app-level HTTP caching (swr / ISR): it conflicted with hydration, so it was left out rather than shipped half-working.
limitations.item4: MapLibre marker clicks aren't covered by pixel-precise E2E tests — Canvas / WebGL projection makes them unreliable to assert on.
limitations.item5: Single-author repository — every pull request was opened, checked by CI, and merged by the same person; no second reviewer.

learned.heading: What I took away
learned.item1: Designing a simulation you can throw away: a deterministic, stateless telemetry source behind an interface, so swapping in a real feed is a config change, not a rewrite.
learned.item2: Treating performance as a contract — per-page Lighthouse budgets in CI — instead of a number you check once and forget.
learned.item3: Keeping an LLM feature honest: structured output, schema validation, IDs grounded in real data, and an eval suite kept separate from the unit tests.
learned.item4: Writing ADRs while deciding, not afterwards — the ones that paid off most were the boring ones (Pinia scope, rendering strategy).

caseStudyChargeHub.title: Case Study: ChargeHub — Mihaela Aghirculesei
caseStudyChargeHub.description: How a solo developer built ChargeHub, an EV charge-point operator dashboard on Nuxt 4: real Open Charge Map data through a server-side BFF, deterministic simulated telemetry behind a swappable interface, a Zod-validated natural-language search on Claude Haiku, seven ADRs, and per-page Lighthouse budgets enforced in CI.
